newsitem.title: UK: Rumours of central bank sales rock gold market. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Rumours of central bank sales rock gold market. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]

text.p: Rumours that a central bank has been selling gold from its reserves increased in intensity on Thursday after heavy sales rocked prices in the Far East and early European markets.
Bullion fixed at its lowest price in over three years earlier this week in a market ignored by speculators and discouraged by selling from almost anybody who owns a few gold bars.
And the biggest worry of all is that one or more of the central banks has been behind the sales.
"There are a lot of guessing games going on at the moment," said bullion analyst Andy Smith at Union Bank of Switzerland.
Confirming that a central bank has been selling is almost impossible. "Anonymity is critical for the central bank," said Smith.

"The intelligence we've had is that it (selling) is generally not coming from producers...We can only presume it's either new positioning going short through the speculators or, more likely some central bank disposals," Chris Fehon, global head of precious metals for Citibank in Sydney said on Thursday.
The central banks and other "institutional" gold holders like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) have around 35,000 tonnes of gold in the vaults.

According to a survey completed last year by former South African Reserve Bank official James Cross, only about 2,100 tonnes of that metal is actively employed either through lending to the market or used as the backing for options.
The cost of holding gold in reserves even just for the top 10 gold holding central banks totals over $15 billion per year in lost interest earnings, according to Smith.
As talk of central bank sales increased in volume, the gold market's attention began to focus on the European central banks.
The banks were believed to be looking at their reserves as a potential source of funding to help their governments meet the economic criteria necessary for European Monetary Union.

"It has energised a reaction which you cannot put a lid on," said Smith. "Everybody is watching this European thing. Whatever they do with gold, they are not going to buy more. It is just a question of how much less gold they need."

Among the criteria are an inflation rate of no more than 1.5 percentage points above the mean of the three European states with lowest 1997 inflation (corrects inflation criterion) and government debt should not total more than 60 percent of a country's gross domestic product (GDP) and government deficit to GDP ratio should not be above 3 (corrects from 1.5) percent.

The prime suspects became Belgium and Portugal, the former because it has sold over 700 tonnes of gold from reserves since 1989 and the latter following a statement by its finance minister recently apparently suggesting that it would consider parting with some of its reserves.
Portugal denied on Wednesday that it had sold any gold and a Belgian government official has said his government has no intention of selling more gold.
"Nobody will ever admit to being involved in a central bank sale. It's more than a broker's life is worth," said one bullion market source.
Usually the central bank will announce it has sold metal from its reserves weeks or months after the event and the reduction in reserves will show up in IMF statistics.
